title: How Do People Experience You?
author: Pursuing Pragmatic Leadership
summary: Taking a month-long break from work for the first time in a decade, this leader discovered that stepping away from problem-solving left a hole he identified as part of his 'leadership identity,' which prompted a reframing question he now applies both at home and at work: how do I want people to experience my presence, not just what do I do? The essay's central move is distinguishing leadership-as-action (communicating, deciding, giving feedback) from leadership-as-experience (what it feels like to be in the room with someone), arguing that intentions and impact frequently diverge without the leader noticing, especially under stress. He complicates his own framework by noting that the same behavior lands differently on different people — directness read as refreshing by one person and intimidating by another — and resolves this not by becoming inconsistent but by asking what a given person, in a given moment, actually needs from him. The piece closes by observing that neither his children nor the people he has led will remember his decisions or meetings; they will remember what it felt like to be around him, making 'presence' the leadership legacy that actually persists.
points: A month away from work surfaced that the author's sense of leadership identity was tied to solving problems, and its absence produced discomfort even while intentionally resting.

The essay distinguishes leadership actions (communicating, deciding, giving feedback) from leadership as it is experienced by others, arguing the latter often diverges from intent without the leader's awareness, especially under stress.

It gives four concrete intention/experience mismatches: intending high standards but being experienced as impossible to please, intending help but being experienced as controlling, intending autonomy but being experienced as unsupportive, and intending decisiveness but being experienced as dismissive.
The author explicitly rejects a one-size-fits-all approach to presence, since identical behavior (e.g. directness) can be experienced as refreshing by one person and intimidating by another.

The essay's resolution is not to perform different personas situationally, but to ask which of one's genuine traits a specific person and moment calls for -- reframed as awareness and adaptability rather than inconsistency.
quotes: But taking a month off work left me feeling as though part of my leadership identity was missing.
My kids don't need the CEO version of me. They don't need every problem solved or every moment optimized. Sometimes they need me to be playful, patient, curious, or firm.
You may intend to hold high standards, but someone may experience you as impossible to please. You may intend to help, but someone may experience you as controlling.
Those experiences shape behavior, and repeated over time, they contribute to culture. In other words, how people experience our presence becomes part of the environment we lead.

One person may experience directness as refreshing. Another may experience the same conversation as intimidating. One teammate may thrive when given a lot of autonomy. Another may interpret that distance as a lack of support.
My kids won't someday evaluate my leadership philosophy. Instead, they'll have an answer to a much simpler question: What did it feel like when Dad was in the room?
